# vLLM Engine & GPU Optimization

## What is vLLM
- High-throughput, memory-efficient inference and serving engine (UC Berkeley)
- Open-source community-driven: 1.5k+ contributors, 10.3k forks, 58.5k+ GitHub stars

![][image3]
- Supports CUDA and HIP (AMD ROCm)
- Optimized pre-built vLLM dockers for AMD GPUs
- Continuous CI/CD tests for vLLM on AMD GPUs
- Optimized high-performance AMD ROCm GPU kernels: AITER, Composable Kernel, hipBLASLt, RCCL
- Optimized OpenAI Triton AMD backend support for vLLM Triton codes
- Continuous support for vLLM new features on AMD GPUs

## vLLM Speed Features
- Efficient management of attention KV cache
- Continuous batching of incoming requests
- Fast model execution with CUDA/HIP graph
- Quantization support: Int8, FP8, and FP4
- Optimized high-performance GPU kernels
- New inference algorithms

## Core Features

### PagedAttention
- Virtualizes KV cache with paging (like OS virtual memory)
- Minimal memory fragmentation
- Supports long context + large batches

### Continuous Batching
- Dynamically inserts new requests into active batches
- Keeps GPU fully utilized
- Ideal for high-concurrency workloads

### Optimized GPU Kernels
- Optimized attention and GEMM kernels
- Efficient decoding at scale
- Optional deterministic (batch-invariant) mode

| Feature | Benefit |
|---------|---------|
| Prefix prefill | Accelerated prompt ingestion, reduced prefill latency |
| Batch invariance | Same prompt + seed → same output regardless of batch size, ordering, concurrency. Critical for reproducibility & evaluation |

## OpenAI-Compatible Server API
- FastAPI-based server for online serving
- Deploy at scale without changing much underneath

## Optimized Execution Loop (vLLM V1)
- Separates CPU and GPU intensive workloads into different processes
- Enables higher compute utilization
- Especially important for multimodal LLM performance (heavily relies on CPU for preprocessing)

![][image4]

## Architecture / Entrypoints

![][image14]
| Mode | Use Case |
|------|----------|
| Offline (`LLM` class, Python API) | Local/batch inference, evaluation, preprocessing scripts |
| Online (HTTP API) | High-concurrency production serving, scales across users and workloads |

```python
from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B")
outputs = llm.generate(["Hello, my name is", "The capital of France is"])
```

## Scheduler
- Simple and flexible: manages token allocations in a fixed budget
- No distinction between prefill-only and decode-only phases
- Scheduling decisions as simple dict: `{request_id: num_tokens}`
- General enough for chunked prefills, prefix caching, speculative decoding
- Users benefit from shorter prompt token response latency

![][image5]
![][image6]

## Benchmarking Tools
| Tool | Script |
|------|--------|
| Online benchmark | `vllm bench serve` |
| Offline benchmark | `vllm bench throughput` |
| Structured output | `benchmarks/benchmark_serving_structured_output.py` |
| Long document QA | `benchmarks/benchmark_long_document_qa_throughput.py` |
| Prefix caching | `benchmarks/benchmark_prefix_caching.py` |
| Request prioritization | `benchmarks/benchmark_prioritization.py` |

### Benchmark Types
- **Latency**: evaluates without parallelism — measures token latency for individual requests, highlights baseline performance, ideal for low-load scenarios
- **Throughput**: focuses on batch processing (e.g., 4-way tensor parallelism), fixed-length output, measures raw tokens/sec. Batch processing processes multiple requests simultaneously — maximizes hardware usage but increases individual request latency. For interactive high-volume tasks
- **Online**: tests with synthetic random data — measures TTFT, TPOT, ITL, E2EL for responsiveness and stability

## Evaluation Metrics
| Metric | Definition |
|--------|-----------|
| TTFT | Time to First Token — initial delay from send to first output piece |
| TPOT | Time Per Output Token — avg time to generate each new token after first |
| ITL | Inter-Token Latency — delay between consecutive tokens arriving |
| E2EL | End-to-End Latency — total time from request to complete response |

## AMD ROCm GPU Optimization

### ROCm Stack
- ROCm required to run AMD GPUs; vLLM needs AITER to work directly with hardware
- Model runs in a Docker container

![][image25]

### Tensor Parallelism
- Splits weight matrices across multiple GPUs (e.g., column-wise split → concatenate outputs)
- Required for models too large for single GPU memory

### HIP Graphs
- Pre-records sequences of GPU operations fused into one action
- vLLM pre-builds graphs for different input sizes and lengths
- `max_seq_len_to_capture`: if sequence length exceeds this → falls back to eager mode (each operation launched individually, slower)

![][image26]

### Attention Sinks
- Specific tokens (often the first few) that attract disproportionate attention due to softmax normalization
- Act as anchors in attention distribution

![][image27]
- Evicting them from KV cache → model loses anchor → quality degrades rapidly
- Keeping sink tokens while evicting others allows good output even with sliding window attention
- Prefix caching with eviction needs to protect attention sinks
- AITER currently doesn't support identifying sink tokens during cache eviction

### KV Cache Optimization
- FP16 → FP8 KV cache reduces memory, allows more concurrent users and longer sequences
- **Trade-off**: adds dequantization latency (FP16→FP8 on the fly) — only beneficial under high concurrency. With one/few users, you're adding latency. Understand your user base
- PagedAttention `block_size` parameter controls KV cache block granularity

### Chunked Prefill
- Default: enabled (prioritizes throughput for multiple concurrent users)
- For max throughput with single/few users: disable chunking

![][image33]
![][image34]
![][image35]
![][image36]

### Sliding Window
- Prevents KV cache from exploding in size for long sequences

![][image28]

### Async Scheduling
- Works asynchronously — essential in times of high load

### AITER (AI Tensor Engine for ROCm)
- Provides optimized HIP kernels specific to AMD architectures
- When disabled: falls back to generic PyTorch/Triton code
- When enabled: uses architecture-specific code, speeding up lower-level operations

![][image37]

**Fused kernel** (enabled by AITER flag) combines:
1. **FP8 KV cache dequantization**: converts 8-bit keys/values back to higher precision before attention
2. **RoPE application**: Rotary Position Embeddings — transformers process tokens in parallel, RoPE rotates each vector based on position to encode relative distance. Normally these run separately; fused kernel handles both automatically

![][image38]

### Key Environment Variables
| Variable | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_LINEAR=1` | Optimized linear layers for Q/K/V projections. Default math routines are correct but not fully optimized for AMD; this flag maximizes throughput and minimizes latency |
| `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT=1` | Use hipBLASLt (faster bf16/fp8 matmuls) over rocBLAS. LLMs spend much time on matrix multiplications (GEMM, attention, feedforward layers — backbone of transformer inference) |

![][image39]
| `AITER_MHA=1` | Flash attention (default); `0` = Triton fallback |
| `HIP_FORCE_DEV_KERNARG` | Copy kernel args to GPU memory — small per-kernel win |

### GPU Memory Utilization
- Default `gpu-memory-utilization=0.9` (can increase for better performance)
- Remaining ~10% used for:
  - **HIP Graphs**: fused operation workflows (6-8 GB). If insufficient room, recording takes long
  - **PyTorch fragmentation**: unaligned variable space (2-4 GB)
  - **Kernel workspace**: temporary matmul storage (1-2 GB)

## DeepSeek Deployment on AMD GPUs

### Kernel Fusion Driver (KFD)
- Without KFD, frameworks like PyTorch and HIP have no way to submit work to the GPU

![][image29]

### Distributed Communication
| Backend | Role |
|---------|------|
| GLOO (`GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0`) | CPU-based process coordination, initialization, sync. Use even with single GPU |
| NCCL/RCCL (`NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0`) | High-performance GPU collective ops (all-reduce for gradient sync). RCCL = AMD equivalent of NVIDIA's NCCL |

Both used together: GLOO for control/setup, NCCL/RCCL for moving large GPU tensors efficiently.

![][image30]

### Key Launch Flags
- `--trust-remote-code`: gives permission to run model authors' scripts — allows model to stay up-to-date and compatible with vLLM

![][image31]
![][image32]
- `--max-num-seqs 512`: pipeline size — many GPU instructions precomputed by vLLM for speed
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`: reduces KV cache to 8-bit (see trade-offs above)
